title: Built To Crash: The UAE's Eight-Year, One-Way Trip to a Red Asteroid
excerpt: A small probe has no engine to slow it down and no way to be steered from Earth. If it works, the mission could reveal what one of the solar system’s strangest asteroids is made of.
content:
In 2028, a small UAE-built probe is scheduled to begin an eight-year journey to the asteroid 269 Justitia. Its final descent is expected to last only two to three hours, and its last act will be crashing into it and transmitting a final photo.

The mission is also a test of whether the UAE can build the systems, expertise and teams that more ambitious exploration will demand.

At first glance, the probe is a small object fixed to the bottom of a larger spacecraft – it is hardly noticeable on the half-scale model on display, so much so that Dr Anton Ivanov, principal investigator and executive director, Propulsion and Space Research Center, Technology Innovation Institute (TII), has to go out of his way to point it out to me.

Despite its modest scale, Ivanov recalls a simple checklist his team went through during a design review: “Does it have its own battery? Yes. Does it have its own communication system? Yes. Does it have its own attitude control? Yes. Does it have its own instruments? Yes. So yeah, it is a spacecraft.”

This probe was built to separate from the larger spacecraft and operate independently. The distinction is relevant because by the time it reaches Justitia, the probe will be far beyond the reach of real-time intervention. Whatever happens, happens.

The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) is the UAE’s second interplanetary mission. The MBR Explorer spacecraft is scheduled to launch from Japan in March 2028 and travel roughly five billion kilometres. It will use gravity assists at Venus, Earth and Mars and fly past six asteroids before Justitia, where it is expected to reach by 2036.

After launch, the probe receives no commands from Earth. TII says it also takes images during the cruise, sending data back about every six months.

The route is only part of the challenge. The spacecraft must cope with wildly varying conditions, from the heat near Mars and close to the sun, and the cold of the asteroid belt. The team behind the mission describes a system of interdependent parts, where thermal management, navigation, propulsion, software and materials all work together for years.

The challenge is sharpest after separation, when the probe is expected to descend for two to three hours, depending on Justitia’s still-uncertain gravity. A heavier asteroid would mean a faster fall.

What’s the Point?

The missions is aimed at a question both basic and potentially consequential: what is Justitia made of?

It is approximately 50 kilometres across, with a striking red colour leaving room for competing possibilities. “Maybe it’s one [asteroid], maybe it’s a rubble pile. Maybe it’s one big piece of iron. Maybe it’s, you know, something else because it’s so red, so we don’t know. This is why it’s a mission of exploration,” says Ivanov.

It is among the reddest bodies observed in the main asteroid belt, closesly resembling objects in the farther Kuiper Belt. The current theory, as the team describes it, is that it formed in the cold outer solar system and was shifted inwards by gravitational disturbances early in the solar system’s history. This mission could help confirm or deny that theory.

Researchers hope to learn whether water-related minerals or organic compounds have been preserved there, and what they could reveal about how these may have been distributed as the planets formed.

The probe itself carries no instruments for analysing the asteroid’s chemistry. The team says this was a deliberate choice made to keep the probe small and light. It has two cameras – one wide-angle, one narrow, which would capture images during the descent, hoping to show morphology including rocks and crevices. The main spacecraft carries cameras, a thermal instrument and spectrometers to investigate the surface’s composition. Together, the observations are meant to provide both close-up views of the terrain as well as broader scientific measurements.

Brace for Impact

The probe’s camera strategy reflects a practical concern: after release, no one can be certain exactly how it will move. It will likely rotate after separation, the team said in a press conference, in part because its release mechanism will have spent eight years in space, and nobody qualifies such hardware for that long. The attitude-control system is meant to counteract the spin and point the cameras.

Ivanov calls it “kind of experimental” because nobody has flown anything like it. The two cameras were chosen to maximise the chances of capturing the asteroid, with the wide-angle providing a backup in case the probe’s orientation isn’t ideal.

While TII describes the mission as ending in a landing, it is a hard landing. The probe has no propulsion, and mass constraints ruled out a more elaborate soft-landing system, so it will end in an impact. The team does not expect the probe to survive. Its battery is designed to keep operating for an extra 20 to 50 minutes in case it does, so it can transmit its latest data, which they hope will be a close-up shot of the asteroid. The impact may also excavate a small crater, exposing material beneath the surface.

That makes the final images especially valuable. The probe is designed to rank images using AI, sending back the most useful ones. Ivanov explains that it can take more pictures than it can send, making this capability vital to make the most of potentially limited communications windows. If the probe rotates or loses its line of sight with the main spacecraft, transmission could become more difficult.

The team explains that AI doesn’t make decisions regarding guidance and navigation, only where some judgment is acceptable, such as selecting images.

At the centre of this image handling is the probe’s data processing unit (DPU). Ivanov describes it as a locally developed, space-qualified computer with small-scale AI capability. Depending on the software loaded, it could serve as a DPU or a full spacecraft computer. By his comparison, a modern Nvidia graphics card can draw 100-150 watts of power, compared to the DPUs 3 watts.

“This is exactly what we need for our requirements, or what we’re shooting for is developing an AI board, AI-capable board that can withstand space conditions and it’s very, very low power,” Ivanov says. “So this is a very specific niche market that we're targeting.”

The same board, with different software, is being adapted for a lunar rover project, where it could support autonomous navigation near the moon’s south pole. The longer-term ambition is space-ready, low-power computing for other applications.

War in the early part of the year only led to a minor delay, Ivanov says, recalling how everyone continued working despite missile interceptions overhead in Abu Dhabi. Microelectronics due to be delivered on 1 March were delayed when UAE airspace closed, moving the schedule by a couple of weeks, without a major impact on the final project delivery date.
